title: Deployment platforms
summary: Take your AI app off your laptop and put it on the internet, choosing the right hosting platform for the job.
objectives: Explain what deployment means and why localhost is not enough
Tell apart static hosts, app platforms (PaaS), and serverless functions
Match a platform to a project: Streamlit, FastAPI, or a static front end
Configure environment variables and secrets safely on a host
Pin dependencies with requirements.txt for reproducible deploys
Read build logs and diagnose a failed deployment

quiz.q: Why can't you just send a friend your localhost URL to use your app?
quiz.answer: localhost (127.0.0.1) only refers to the machine the request comes from, so it points at their computer, not yours; the app must be hosted on a public server with a real domain.
quiz.why: localhost always resolves to the local machine, so a public, reachable host is required for others to access your app.

quiz.q: Which platform type runs your code only when a request arrives and scales to zero when idle?
quiz.why: Serverless functions spin up on demand per request and cost nothing while idle, but have cold starts and time limits.

quiz.q: Where should your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live when deployed?
options: In the platform's secrets / environment variables settings
In the README so teammates can find it
quiz.why: Secrets belong in the host's environment-variable settings, never in code or version control where they can leak.

quiz.q: What is the main job of requirements.txt during deployment?
options: It lists the Python packages the host must install
quiz.why: The host reads requirements.txt to pip install the exact packages your app needs, making the build reproducible.

quiz.q: Name one trade-off of serverless functions compared with an always-on PaaS app.
quiz.answer: Cold starts: the first request after idle is slow while the function boots; there are also execution time limits unsuited to long-running tasks.
quiz.why: Serverless saves money at idle but adds latency on cold starts and caps how long a single request can run.

quiz.q: A static host like Netlify or GitHub Pages can run your Python FastAPI backend.
quiz.why: False. Static hosts only serve pre-built files (HTML, CSS, JS); running Python server code needs a PaaS or serverless platform.

resources.label: Streamlit Community Cloud — Deploy an app
The Twelve-Factor App — III. Config (env vars)

body_markdown:
## What deployment really means

**Deployment** is moving your app from your laptop to a server that anyone on the internet can reach. While you build, you run things on `localhost` — address `127.0.0.1` — which always means *this machine*. Send that link to a friend and it points at *their* computer, not yours.

To go public you need a **host**: a machine (or managed service) that is always on, has a public address, and runs your code. Your job is to package the app, tell the host how to start it, and hand over your secrets safely.

## Three kinds of platform

Not every app needs the same host. The three families you'll meet:

- **Static hosts** (Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages) — serve pre-built files only: HTML, CSS, JavaScript. No Python runs. Great for a portfolio site or a React front end.
- **Platform-as-a-Service / PaaS** (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Streamlit Cloud, Hugging Face Spaces) — you give it code, it builds and runs a long-lived process. Perfect for a FastAPI or Streamlit AI app.
- **Serverless functions** (Vercel Functions, AWS Lambda) — your code runs only when a request arrives, then scales to zero. Cheap at idle, but **cold starts** add latency and there are time limits.

## Pinning dependencies

The host is a fresh machine — none of your packages are installed. A `requirements.txt` lists exactly what to install so the build is reproducible.

```bash
pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt
# anthropic==0.39.0
# fastapi==0.115.0
# uvicorn==0.32.0
```

## Secrets and environment variables

Never hard-code an API key, and never commit a `.env` file. Read keys from the environment, and set the real values in the platform's secrets panel.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one line."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Picking a platform

For this course, **Streamlit Community Cloud** and **Hugging Face Spaces** are the fastest free routes to a live AI demo — connect a GitHub repo and they build it for you. Reach for **Render** when you need a plain FastAPI backend with a public URL. Use a static host only for a front end with no Python.

## Your task

Pick one app you've built. Write its `requirements.txt`, move every secret to an environment variable, push to GitHub, and deploy it to Streamlit Cloud or Hugging Face Spaces. Share the live link.

slides.title: Deployment platforms
slides.sub: Month 5 - Polish, Deploy, Go Public  |  Lesson 1
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Five, where we polish your work, deploy it, and go public. In this first lesson we tackle deployment platforms. By the end you'll understand what it really means to put an app online, the three main kinds of hosting platform, and how to choose the right one for your A I project. This is the step that turns a project on your laptop into something you can show the world.

slides.title: What is deployment?
bullets: Moving your app from laptop to a public server.
localhost (127.0.0.1) means 'this machine' only.
A host is always on with a public address.
slides.narration: So what does deployment actually mean? Up to now you've run everything on localhost, address one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one, which always means this machine, your own computer. If you send that link to a friend it points at their machine, not yours. Deployment means moving the app onto a host: a server that is always on and has a public address anyone can reach.

slides.title: Static hosts
bullets: Serve pre-built files: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
No Python runs on the server.
Netlify, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages.
Great for a portfolio or front end.
slides.narration: The first family is static hosts, like Netlify, GitHub Pages, and Cloudflare Pages. These serve files that are already built: H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript. No Python ever runs on the server, it just hands files to the browser. They're perfect for a portfolio site or a front end, but they cannot run your A I backend.

slides.title: Platform-as-a-Service
bullets: You give it code; it builds and runs it.
Runs a long-lived process for you.
Render, Railway, Streamlit Cloud, HF Spaces.
Ideal for FastAPI or Streamlit AI apps.
slides.narration: The second family is Platform as a Service, or P A A S. You hand it your code, and it builds and runs a long-lived process for you, no servers to manage by hand. Render, Railway, Streamlit Cloud, and Hugging Face Spaces all live here. This is your default choice for a FastAPI or Streamlit A I app, because something needs to keep running to answer requests.

slides.title: Serverless functions
bullets: Code runs only when a request arrives.
Scales to zero when idle, so cheap.
Cold starts add latency; time limits apply.
Vercel Functions, AWS Lambda.
slides.narration: The third family is serverless functions, such as Vercel Functions and A W S Lambda. Here your code runs only when a request comes in, then scales right down to zero when nobody's using it, so it's very cheap at idle. The trade-offs are cold starts, where the first request after a quiet spell is slow while the function boots, and limits on how long a single request can run.

slides.title: Pin your dependencies
bullets: The host starts as a fresh, empty machine.
requirements.txt lists packages to install.
pip freeze captures exact versions.
slides.code:
pip freeze > requirements.txt
# anthropic==0.39.0
# fastapi==0.115.0
# uvicorn==0.32.0
slides.narration: Remember that the host is a brand new, empty machine, none of your packages are installed. You tell it what to install with a file called requirements dot t x t. Running pip freeze captures the exact versions you used and writes them out. Pinning versions like this makes your build reproducible, so it works the same way every time.

slides.title: Keep secrets safe
bullets: Never hard-code keys or commit a .env file.
Read keys from environment variables.
Set real values in the host's secrets panel.
slides.code:
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
slides.narration: Secrets like your A P I key must never be hard-coded in your code or committed to git in a dot env file, that's how keys leak. Instead, read them from the environment. The Anthropic client picks up ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY automatically. Then you set the real value in the platform's secrets or environment-variables panel, separate from your code.

slides.title: Which platform?
bullets: Streamlit Cloud or HF Spaces: fastest free AI demo.
Render: plain FastAPI backend with a public URL.
Static host: front end only, no Python.
Connect a GitHub repo and it builds for you.
slides.narration: So which do you pick? For a quick, free A I demo, Streamlit Community Cloud and Hugging Face Spaces are the fastest routes, you just connect a GitHub repo and they build it for you. Reach for Render when you need a plain FastAPI backend with a public U R L. And use a static host only when there's no Python at all, just a front end.

slides.title: When a deploy fails
bullets: Read the build logs from the top.
Most failures are missing packages or bad versions.
Check secrets are set on the host, not just locally.
Confirm the start command matches your app.
slides.narration: Your first deploy will probably fail, and that's completely normal. The build logs are your friend, read them from the top, because the first error is usually the real one. Most failures are a missing package in requirements, a wrong version, a secret you forgot to set on the host, or a start command that doesn't match your app. Fix one thing, redeploy, repeat.

bullets: Deployment puts your app on a public host.
Three families: static, PaaS, serverless.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Deployment moves your app off localhost onto a public host. There are three families: static hosts for files, P A A S for long-running apps, and serverless for on-demand functions. You pin your packages in requirements dot t x t and keep secrets in environment variables, never in code. For an A I demo, Streamlit Cloud or Hugging Face Spaces are the easiest. Your task: deploy one app you've built and share the live link. See you in the next lesson.
